payload.throughline: Read side-chain chemistry and charge first, then trace how covalent links, aqueous interactions, and sequence constraints shape peptide and protein behavior.

curriculum_context.canonical_title: Explain amino-acid control of protein structure

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: distinguish a hydrocarbon-rich side chain from a side chain carrying a charged group.
Purpose: you will be able to infer interaction tendencies from side-chain chemistry rather than recall isolated amino-acid names.

Hydrocarbon-rich side chains are generally hydrophobic. Polar uncharged side chains can interact with water through dipoles or hydrogen bonds. Acidic side chains tend to carry negative charge when deprotonated; basic side chains tend to carry positive charge when protonated under the stated condition.

Hydrophobic residues often favor burial away from water, while polar or charged residues often favor aqueous exposure. Opposite charges can attract; like charges repel; hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors can stabilize compatible geometry.
Mental model — functional group, charge, water, partner: classify the chemical group first, then predict its solvent preference and compatible interaction.

Think aloud: a side chain ends in a deprotonated carboxylate. It is negatively charged and hydrophilic, so an aqueous surface or attraction to a positive group is more plausible than burial in a nonpolar core.
Worked nonpolar case: a side chain dominated by carbon-hydrogen bonds lacks charge and strong hydrogen-bonding groups, so it tends to favor hydrophobic packing.
Worked polar case: a neutral hydroxyl-containing side chain can hydrogen-bond with water and compatible protein groups without carrying formal charge.
Guided practice: classify a deprotonated carboxylate side chain.
Less help: classify a neutral amide or hydroxyl side chain as hydrophilic.
On your own: select a likely interaction partner for a charged side chain.
Boundary: hydrophilic does not always mean charged, and acidic does not mean the entire amino acid is always negative at every pH. Use the stated condition.
Near exit: classify a fresh side-chain functional group and predict its aqueous interaction.
Changed-task exit: predict the structural consequence of replacing a buried hydrophobic side chain with a charged side chain.
Repair classification: identify formal charge first, then polar groups, then hydrocarbon surface.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different side chain and interaction tendency.
Repair mutation reasoning: hold protein location fixed, compare old and new solvent preference, and predict whether the local environment remains compatible.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same environment-compatibility reasoning to a surface mutation.
Recap from memory: distinguish acidic, basic, polar uncharged, and hydrophobic side chains and name one interaction favored by each.
One chemistry-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each failed function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: identify the dipolar form that carries both ammonium and carboxylate groups.
Purpose: you will be able to keep formal charge state separate from three-dimensional α-carbon configuration.

Amino acids can exist as dipolar ions with a protonated amino group and deprotonated carboxyl group. Under strongly acidic conditions, greater protonation tends toward positive net charge; under strongly basic conditions, greater deprotonation tends toward negative net charge.

For absolute configuration, assign priorities using the supplied order, orient the lowest-priority group away, and trace 1→2→3: clockwise is R and counterclockwise is S. Glycine lacks a chiral α carbon; cysteine can differ from the common L-amino-acid pattern because sulfur changes priority.
Mental model — charge ledger and orientation ledger: sum formal charges for ionic state; orient priority 4 away before tracing configuration.
Think aloud: NH₃⁺ and COO⁻ with an uncharged side chain sum to zero but remain dipolar. Net zero does not mean no formal charges.
Worked charge case: at a condition with NH₃⁺ and COO⁻, the backbone contributes +1 and −1, yielding net zero before any side-chain charge.
Worked configuration case: with group 4 away, a clockwise 1→2→3 sequence is R; if group 4 points toward the viewer, the apparent result must be inverted.
Guided practice: sum formal charges in a stated zwitterionic structure.
Less help: predict the direction of net charge in strongly acidic solution.
On your own: identify whether an α carbon is chiral from four substituents.
Boundary: net-zero zwitterion is not uncharged at every atom, and L/D notation is not assigned by simply reading R/S without the supplied stereochemical relation.
Near exit: determine a fresh net charge from explicit protonation states.
Changed-task exit: switch to a supplied three-dimensional priority trace and determine α-carbon configuration.
Repair charge state: write each formal charge and add them, including any ionizable side chain stated in the prompt.
Fresh re-entry: apply the charge ledger under a different pH condition.
Repair configuration: identify priority 4, orient it away, trace 1→2→3, and invert only when 4 points toward.
Fresh re-entry: apply that orientation sequence to a different supplied trace.
Recap from memory: define a zwitterion, predict acidic and basic charge directions, and state the bounded R/S assignment sequence.
One charge or orientation cue and one untouched re-entry bound each failed function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: identify the covalent bond joining amino-acid residues in a peptide backbone.
Purpose: you will be able to choose the bond-specific chemistry before predicting a peptide or sulfur-link outcome.

A peptide bond is an amide linkage between the carboxyl carbon of one residue and the amino nitrogen of the next. Condensation forms the link with water loss; hydrolysis adds water across the bond and separates the connected fragments.

Oxidation of two cysteine thiols can form a cystine disulfide bond. Reduction cleaves the S−S bond back toward thiols. Peptide hydrolysis and disulfide reduction target different covalent bonds and produce different outcomes.
Mental model — name the bond, name the reaction, conserve the chain: amide plus hydrolysis splits the backbone; disulfide plus reduction removes a cross-link.
Think aloud: the reagent is reducing and the diagram highlights S−S, so I predict loss of the disulfide cross-link, not peptide-backbone cleavage.
Worked peptide case: complete hydrolysis of a tripeptide cleaves two peptide bonds and yields three amino-acid residues in their condition-dependent ionic forms.
Worked sulfur case: oxidizing two cysteine side-chain thiols forms one disulfide link; reducing that link restores two sulfur-containing termini.
Guided practice: identify the atoms connected by a peptide bond.
Less help: count peptide bonds in a short linear chain.
On your own: predict complete peptide hydrolysis fragments.
Boundary: reducing a disulfide does not hydrolyze every peptide bond, and peptide hydrolysis does not by itself specify disulfide reduction.
Near exit: count cleavage and products in a fresh linear peptide hydrolysis.
Changed-task exit: switch bond type and predict the effect of a reducing environment on a disulfide-stabilized protein.
Repair hydrolysis: count residue-to-residue links as n−1 for a linear n-residue peptide, then split only the named links.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same counting function to a different chain length.
Repair sulfur chemistry: oxidation forms S−S; reduction breaks S−S. Keep the peptide backbone unchanged unless separately hydrolyzed.
Fresh re-entry: apply that bond-specific rule to a different interchain disulfide.
Recap from memory: define peptide formation and hydrolysis, relate residue count to linear bond count, and contrast disulfide oxidation with reduction.
One bond-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: distinguish amino-acid sequence from a local α-helix or β-sheet pattern.
Purpose: you will be able to trace a sequence or environmental change to the protein structural level and interaction it affects first.

Primary structure is amino-acid sequence. Secondary structure includes local backbone patterns such as α helices and β sheets stabilized mainly by backbone hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional fold of one chain; quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple chains.

In water, hydrophobic side chains often pack inward while polar and charged groups often remain solvated or form compatible interactions. Proline can disrupt regular backbone geometry; cystine disulfides can stabilize folds. Heat, extreme pH, or solvent changes can denature higher structure without necessarily hydrolyzing primary peptide sequence.
Mental model — level, interaction, environment: locate the changed bond or contact, identify whether it is within sequence, local backbone, one chain, or between chains, then predict stability.
Think aloud: heat disrupts many noncovalent interactions but the prompt preserves peptide bonds. I predict loss of secondary and tertiary organization while primary sequence remains.
Worked aqueous folding: nonpolar side chains cluster away from water while polar groups remain exposed or form internal hydrogen bonds when geometry is favorable.
Worked mutation: replacing a helix-interior residue with proline can kink the backbone and disrupt local secondary structure, which may propagate to tertiary stability.
Guided practice: map an α helix to secondary structure.
Less help: identify tertiary versus quaternary interactions.
On your own: predict hydrophobic burial in aqueous solution.

Boundary: denaturation is not automatically peptide hydrolysis. A disulfide is covalent tertiary or quaternary stabilization, while ordinary backbone hydrogen bonds are noncovalent secondary stabilization.
Near exit: identify the first structural level affected by a fresh localized interaction change.
Changed-task exit: predict which levels remain after an environmental denaturant disrupts noncovalent interactions but leaves peptide bonds intact.
Repair structural level: ask whether the changed feature is sequence, local backbone pattern, one-chain fold, or multi-chain interface.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different interaction at a different structural level.
Repair denaturation reasoning: list bond classes preserved and disrupted before naming which structural levels remain.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same preservation analysis to reduction of disulfides with noncovalent contacts otherwise maintained.
Recap from memory: define all four structural levels and explain roles for hydrophobic interactions, solvation, proline, cystine, and denaturation.
One level-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
